en: The Parivāra:
The Analysis of the Bhikkhunī Rules,
First Part
2.1 The Section on the Formulation of Rules (Katthapaññattivāra) 1.
The Chapter on Defeat (Pārājikakaṇḍa):
Where was the fifth offense entailing defeat for bhikkhunīs formulated by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One?
With reference to whom?
On what basis? Is there therein a formal rule (paññatti), a supplementary rule (anupaññatti), or a rule for an unarisen offense (anuppannapaññatti)?
Is it a rule of universal application or a rule of limited application?
Is it a common rule or an uncommon rule?
Is it a rule promulgated on one side or a rule promulgated on both sides?
In which of the four recitations of the Pātimokkha is it included, and in which category is it contained?
By which recitation does it come to be recited?
To which of the four failures does it belong?
Of the seven classes of offenses, which class of offense is it?
Of the six origins of offenses, by how many origins does it originate?
Of the four legal issues, which legal issue is it?
By how many of the seven methods of settling is it settled?
What therein is the Vinaya?
What therein is the further Vinaya?
What therein is the Pātimokkha?
What therein is the higher Pātimokkha?
What is failure?
What is the attainment?
What is the practice?
For how many reasons did the Blessed One lay down the fifth *pārājika* offense for the bhikkhunīs?
Who trains? Who has trained in the training?
Wherein is it established?
Who preserves it?
Whose word is it?
By whom was it brought?
Where was this fifth *pārājika* offense for bhikkhunīs laid down by that Blessed One—who knows and sees, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning the bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā. On what basis?
On the basis that the bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā, being lustful, consented to physical contact with a lustful man; on that basis.
Is there therein a rule (paññatti), a supplementary rule (anupaññatti), and a rule not yet promulgated (anuppannapaññatti)?
There is one rule;
there is no supplementary rule and no rule not yet promulgated therein.
Is it a rule of universal application or a rule of limited application?
It is a rule of universal application.
Is it a common rule or an uncommon rule?
Is it an uncommon designation?
Is it a designation from one side or a designation from both sides?
It is a designation from one side.
In which of the four recitations of the Pātimokkha is it included, and to which does it belong?
It is included in the Introduction (Nidāna) and belongs to the Introduction.
By which recitation does it come to be recited?
It comes under the heading by the second summary.
Of the four failures, which failure is it?
It is failure in virtue.
Of the seven classes of offenses, which class of offense is it?
It is the class of offenses involving defeat (pārājika).
Of the six origins of offenses, by how many origins does it originate?
It originates from one origin:
it originates from both body and mind, but not from speech.
Among the four kinds of legal issues, which kind of legal issue is it?
The legal issue concerning offenses:
by how many of the seven principles for settling disputes is it settled?
It is settled by two principles for settling disputes.
By means of settlement in the presence of the accused (*sammukhāvinaya*) and by means of acting according to what is admitted (*paṭiññātakaraṇa*).
What therein is the discipline (*vinaya*), and what therein is the further discipline (*abhivinaya*)?
The formulation (*paññatti*) is the discipline; the analysis (*vibhatti*) is the further discipline.
What therein is the Pātimokkha, and what therein is the Adhipātimokkha?
The formulation is the Pātimokkha; the exposition is the Adhipātimokkha.
What is failure (vipatti)?
Non-restraint is failure.
What is success?
Restraint is success.
What is the practice?
It is that one undertakes and trains in the rules of training for as long as life lasts, until the end of one’s days, thinking:
“I shall not do such a thing. For how many reasons did the Blessed One prescribe the fifth *pārājika* offense for bhikkhunīs?
The Blessed One laid down the fifth *pārājika* offense for bhikkhunīs based on ten reasons:
for the well-being of the Saṅgha, for the comfort of the Saṅgha, for the restraint of wayward bhikkhunīs, for the ease of living of well-behaved bhikkhunīs,
for the restraint of taints pertaining to the present life, and for those pertaining to future lives...

For the restraint of the taints, for the inspiration of those without confidence, for the increase of those with confidence, for the endurance of the true Dhamma, and for the support of the discipline.
Who train? Both those in training (sekkhā) and the virtuous worldlings (puthujjanakalyāṇika) train.
Who are those who have trained in the training?
The Arahants are those who have trained in the training.
Where is it established?
It is established among those who desire training.
Who are they that uphold it?
Those in whom it is practiced are the ones who uphold it.
Whose word is it?
It is the word of the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
By whom was it brought?
Transmitted through succession:
Upāli, Dāsaka,
Soṇaka, and likewise Siggava.
Moggaliputta was the fifth;
these [five] were in the land called Jambusiri.
Then Mahinda and Itthiya,
Uttiyo, Sambalo likewise,
and the wise one named Bhadda—
these were nāgas of great wisdom.
They came here from Jambudīpa;
they recited the Vinaya,
the Piṭaka of Tambapaṇṇi.
They recited the five Nikāyas and the seven treatises;
then the wise Ariṭṭha—
And Tissa-datta the wise,
Visāraḍa Kāḷasumana,
and the elder named Dīgha;
And the wise Dīghasumana;
again, Kāḷasumana,
the Elder Nāga, and Buddharakkhita.
The wise elder Tissa and the learned elder Deva;
furthermore, the wise Sumanas.
Confident in the Vinaya,
the learned Cūḷanāga is as unassailable as an elephant.
And he named Dhammapālita,
who was highly honored in Rohaṇa;
his disciple was one of great wisdom.
Named Khema, a master of the three Piṭakas,
you shone forth with wisdom like the king of stars in the sky.
Upatissa was wise,
and Phussadeva was a great speaker;
furthermore, Sumana was wise.
Named Puppha, he was of great learning;
a great orator and a great sage,
he was skilled in all the Piṭakas.
Furthermore, Upāli was wise,
confident in the Vinaya,
a great nāga of vast intelligence.
Skilled in the lineage of the true Dhamma,
the wise Abhaya was likewise proficient in all the Piṭakas.
And the wise Elder Tissa was confident in the Vinaya;
his disciple was of great wisdom.
Named Puppha, he was of great learning;
protecting the Dispensation,
he was established in Jambudīpa.
And the wise Cūḷābhaya,
confident in the Vinaya,
and the wise Elder Tissa—
Skilled in the lineage of the true Dhamma,
the wise Cūḷadeva was also confident in the Vinaya.
And the wise Elder Siva,
skilled in all matters of the Vinaya—
these are Nāgas of great wisdom.
Knowing the Vinaya and skilled in the Path,
they proclaimed the Vinaya Pitaka on Tambapaṇṇi.
Where was this sixth *pārājika* offense for bhikkhunīs laid down by the Blessed One—who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning the bhikkhunī Thullanandā.
In what matter? In this matter:
the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, knowing that another bhikkhunī had committed an offense entailing defeat (pārājika), neither reproached her herself nor informed the community. In that matter.
There is one classification.
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin—it originates from body, speech, and mind. …pe…
Where was the seventh *pārājika* offense for bhikkhunīs laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning the nun Thullanandā.
In regard to what matter?

It was concerning the matter that the nun Thullanandā followed the monk Ariṭṭha—who had formerly been a vulture-trainer—and who had been suspended by a unanimous Saṅgha. It was in regard to that matter.
There is one classification.
It originates from one of the six origins of offenses—namely, by laying down the burden ... [and so forth].
Where was the eighth *pārājika* for bhikkhunīs laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning the group of six bhikkhunīs.
On what basis? On the basis of the eighth matter, which the group of six bhikkhunīs fulfilled. On that basis.
There is one classification.
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin:
through relinquishing the burden … [as above] … .
The eight *pārājika* rules are finished.
Its summary verse is:
Sexual intercourse, taking what is not given, and...
Beyond human contact;
she conceals physical touch;
the eight grounds for suspension.
The Great Hero has laid down the grounds for offense involving cutting off, free from doubt. 2.
The Section on Saṅghādisesa.

Where was this Saṅghādisesa rule laid down by the Blessed One—who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—concerning a nun who brings a legal case as a litigant while making a charge?
Against whom was it directed? On what matter? …pe…
By whom was it brought forth?

Where was the Saṅghādisesa rule laid down by that Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—concerning a nun who brings a legal case as a litigant?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the bhikkhunī Thullanandā.
In regard to what matter?
The nun Thullanandā lived as one who brought false accusations regarding that matter.
Is there therein a formal rule (paññatti), a supplementary rule (anupaññatti), or a rule for an unarisen offense (anuppannapaññatti)?
There is one formal rule.
Therein, there is no subsequent rule (anupaññatti) nor an unarisen rule (anuppannapaññatti).
Is it a universal rule (sabbatthapaññatti) or a partial rule (padesapaññatti)?
It is a universal rule.
Is it a common designation or an uncommon designation?
It is an uncommon designation.
Is it a designation from one side or a designation from both sides?
A single formulation.
In which of the four recitations of the Pātimokkha is it included, and in which is it comprised?
It is included in the Introduction (Nidāna) and comprised within the Introduction.
By which summary does it come under the summary?
It comes under the third summary.
Of the four failures, which failure is it?
Failure in virtue.
Among the seven classes of offenses, to which class of offense does it belong? It belongs to the class of offenses involving formal meeting of the Sangha (saṅghādisesa).
Of the six origins of offenses, by how many origins does it originate?
It originates by two origins:
it may originate from both body and speech, but not from mind.
It may originate from body, speech, and mind...
From whom was it brought? It was brought down through oral tradition.
Upāli, Dāsaka,
Soṇaka, and likewise Siggava;
with Moggaliputta as the fifth—
These, in the land called Jambusiri...
these nāgas of great wisdom.
Knowing the Vinaya and skilled in the Path,
they proclaimed the Vinaya Pitaka on Tambapaṇṇi.
Where was the Saṅghādisesa rule concerning one who causes a nun who has been suspended to leave the suspension declared?
It was declared at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning the bhikkhunī Thullanandā.
On what matter? On the matter of the bhikkhunī Thullanandā ordaining a female thief.
There is one classification.
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from two origins:
it may originate from both speech and mind, but not from body.
It may originate from body, speech, and mind ... [as before] ...
Where was the Saṅghādisesa offense prescribed for one going to another village by oneself?
It was prescribed at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to a certain bhikkhunī.
On account of what matter?
A certain bhikkhunī went alone from one village to another; this is the basis for the rule. There is one original formulation (paññatti) and three subsequent formulations (anupaññatti).
Among the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin: that which originates from a formal act (kammavācā).
In the first *pārājika*... [etc.

... Regarding the offense of *saṅghādisesa* for a nun who reinstates herself without having obtained the permission of the Saṅgha that suspended her by means of a unanimous Saṅgha, in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction, and without knowing the Saṅgha that performed the act or the consent of the group—where was this laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom? With reference to the nun Thullanandā.
In regard to what matter?

The nun Thullanandā, without having obtained the consent of the Saṅgha that had performed the legal act according to Dhamma, Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction, and without knowing the Saṅgha that had carried out the act, reinstated a nun who had been suspended by a unanimous Saṅgha; this was the case regarding that matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Among the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin: [namely, from a formal act].
Regarding the laying down of the burden... [etc.

...Where was it laid down that for a lustful bhikkhunī who, having received with her own hand from the hand of a lustful man, eats either solid food or soft food, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa)?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā.
On account of what matter?
The nun Sundarīnandā, being lustful, accepted food from the hand of a lustful man; this is the matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Among the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin: [the origin of what is done intentionally].
In the first *pārājika*... [etc.
... "Noble lady, what can this man do to you, whether he be lustful or not, since you are free from lust?

Come now, noble lady, whatever fresh or cooked food this man gives you, receive it with your own hand and eat or consume it"—where was this formulated as a *saṅghādisesa* offense for one who incites another in such a manner?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to a certain bhikkhunī.
“In what matter? [It was this:
a certain bhikkhunī said, “What does this man do to you, noble lady, whether he is lustful or not, since you yourself are free from lust?
Come now, noble lady, whatever hard food this man gives you...”
"Or hard food—having received that with your own hand, eat or consume it," he urged him. Regarding this matter:
there is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from three origins …pe… [as above].
Where was the Saṅghādisesa rule laid down for a bhikkhunī who, being angry and displeased, does not relinquish [her position] despite being exhorted up to three times?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning the bhikkhunī Caṇḍakāḷī. On what basis?
On the basis that the bhikkhunī Caṇḍakāḷī, being angry and displeased, spoke thus: “I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dhamma, I renounce the Saṅgha, I renounce the training. It was on this basis.
There is one classification.
Among the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin:
through the laying down of the burden ... [and so on].

In regard to what matter was this Saṅghādisesa rule laid down for a nun who, having been formally charged in some legal case, does not relinquish her position after being admonished up to three times?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning the bhikkhunī Caṇḍakāḷī.
On what matter?
The bhikkhunī Caṇḍakāḷī, having been rebuked in some legal issue, being angry and displeased, spoke thus: “They proceed according to favoritism...”
“...and nuns who follow hatred, and nuns who follow delusion, and nuns who follow fear”—
this was the case. There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin:
by laying down the burden ... [etc.
... Where was the *saṅghādisesa* offense prescribed for those nuns who, being closely associated with laypeople, do not desist even after being admonished up to the third time?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to a number of bhikkhunīs.
In regard to what matter?
It was on account of a number of bhikkhunīs who were living in close association; it was on that matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin:
by laying down the burden...
[as before] ... "Venerable ladies, you should dwell in association."
Where was this Saṅghādisesa rule laid down for one who, when being exhorted up to three times by a woman urging her, saying, “Do not live separately,” does not desist from that course?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning the nun Thullanandā. On what basis?
On the basis that the nun Thullanandā urged them, saying: “Venerable ladies, you should live in association; do not live apart. It was on this basis.
There is one classification.
It originates from one of the six origins of offenses—
namely, by laying down the burden … [and so forth] … .
The ten Saṅghādisesa rules are concluded.
The summary verse for them is:
Usseyya, cori, gāmantaṃ.
And what is raised up by eating?
Why are you angry at anyone?
You are known as one who associates with ten [types of people].
3. The Chapter on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa).

Regarding that which was prescribed by the Blessed One—who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—as a forfeiture offense (nissaggiya-pācittiya) for one who accumulates alms bowls:
where was it laid down? It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the group of six bhikkhunīs.
In regard to what matter?
The group of six bhikkhunīs accumulated almsbowls; this was the case.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Among the six origins of offenses, it originates from two origins: [namely, from desire and from negligence].
Regarding the *kathina* robe... [etc.

... For one who, having determined an out-of-season robe to be an in-season robe, distributes it, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*). Where was this laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the bhikkhunī Thullanandā.
On account of what matter?

The nun Thullanandā, having determined an out-of-season robe to be an in-season robe, caused it to be distributed; this was the case. There is one formal rule (paññatti). Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from three origins … [as before] … *Note: The phrase "ekā paññatti" refers to the specific offense established by this rule. The mention of "six origins of offenses" (cha āpattisamuṭṭhānā) refers to the standard classification of how offenses arise: (1) intention (sañcicca), (2) negligence (pamāda), (3) ignorance (aññāṇa), (4) mental derangement (cittavipallāsa), (5) being forced (sahasakāra), and (6) uncertainty (vimati). The phrase "originates from three origins" indicates that this particular offense arises from the first three.*
Where was the offense of expiation involving forfeiture prescribed for one who, having exchanged a robe with a bhikkhunī, subsequently seizes it back?
It was prescribed at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom was it prescribed?
Concerning the bhikkhunī Thullanandā.
In regard to what matter?
It was on this matter: the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, then took it back. It was on that matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).

Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from three origins … [as before] … For one who, having requested one thing, requests another, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya). Where was this laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the bhikkhunī Thullanandā.
In what matter?
In the matter where the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, having requested one thing, requested another; in that matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from six origins ... [etc. ...
For one who exchanges one thing for another, what is the offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*) prescribed where?
It was prescribed at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the bhikkhunī Thullanandā.
On account of what matter?
The nun Thullanandā, having had one thing bartered for, had another bartered for; this was the case.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
It originates from six origins of offenses; it originates by means of all six origins … [as before] …

"For one who exchanges for something else an article belonging to the Saṅgha that was intended for another purpose and designated for another, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
Where was this laid down? "It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?"
Concerning a number of bhikkhunīs.
In regard to what matter? In regard to this matter:
a number of bhikkhunīs exchanged for something else an article belonging to the Saṅgha that was intended for another purpose and designated for another use. In regard to that matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
It originates from six origins of offenses through six origins [of action] ... [etc. ...

For one who exchanges for something else an article belonging to the Saṅgha that was intended for another purpose and was obtained by solicitation, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya). Where was this laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to a number of bhikkhunīs.
In what matter?

In the matter where several bhikkhunīs, by means of requisites intended for another purpose, designated for another, belonging to the Saṅgha, and obtained through solicitation, bartered them for something else—in that matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).

Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from six origins … [as before] … For one who exchanges for something else a communal requisite intended for another purpose, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture. Where was it laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to a number of bhikkhunīs.
In regard to what matter?

A number of bhikkhunīs exchanged one requisite for another, using what was intended for a specific purpose and designated for a particular individual, when it was actually meant for the community. Regarding this matter:
there is one formal rule (paññatti).
It originates from six origins of offenses; it originates by way of all six origins… [and so on].

"For one who exchanges for something else an article that was intended for another purpose, designated for another, belonging to the community, and obtained by solicitation, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
Where was it laid down? "It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?"
Concerning a number of bhikkhunīs.
In what matter? In this matter:

a number of bhikkhunīs exchanged one requisite for another, using material intended for a different purpose, designated for a specific individual, belonging to a group, and obtained by solicitation. It was in this matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
It originates from six origins of offenses through six origins [of action] ... [etc. ...

For one who exchanges for something else an article intended for another purpose, belonging to an individual, and obtained by her own request, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya). Where was this rule laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the bhikkhunī Thullanandā.
In what matter?
The nun Thullanandā exchanged for something else an article belonging to an individual, which was intended for another purpose, obtained by request; in that matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from six origins ... [as above] ...
For one who causes a heavy cloak worth more than four *karṣa*s to be bartered for, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture. Where was this laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
Concerning whom? Concerning the bhikkhunī Thullanandā.
In regard to what matter?
The nun Thullanandā requested a woolen blanket from the king; this was the case.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
It arises from six origins of offenses; it arises through all six origins …pe….
For one who causes a light cloak worth more than two and a half kaṁsas to be purchased, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture. Where was it laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning the nun Thullanandā. On what basis?
On the basis of the nun Thullanandā requesting linen cloth from a king. On that basis.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
It originates from six origins of offenses through six modes of origination ... [as above] ...
The twelve Nissaggiya Pācittiya rules are finished.
Its summary verse:
The bowl, the improper time, and the proper time,
exchanging, and requesting.
Having caused [cloth] to be sought for another purpose,
or that which belongs to the Sangha or is communal;
[or cloth] obtained by solicitation for an individual.
Four *kaṁsas* and two and a half [more].
4. The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiya-khaṇḍa) 4.1.
The Chapter on Garlic (Lasuṇavagga)
Where was it laid down by that Blessed One—who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—that for one who eats garlic there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning the bhikkhunī Thullanandā. On what basis?
On the basis of the fact that the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, not knowing moderation, had garlic carried away; on that basis.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from two origins: in the case of [the rule concerning] wool... [etc. ...
For one who has hair removed from the private parts, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Where was this rule laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the group of six bhikkhunīs.
In what matter?
The group of six bhikkhunīs had hair removed from the private parts; it was in that matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from four origins ... [and so on] ...
Where was the Pācittiya offense regarding slapping with the palm of the hand prescribed?
It was prescribed at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to two bhikkhunīs.
In regard to what matter?
Two bhikkhunīs clapped their hands; this is the case.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Among the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin: [the offense originates from body and mind].
In the first *pārājika*... [etc. ...
Regarding the *pācittiya* on the use of *jatumaṭṭhaka*: where was it laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to a certain bhikkhunī.
In regard to what matter?
A certain bhikkhunī took resin-impregnated cloth; this is the case.
There is one rule.
